entries.bf3f0a3e39aeb126fb6cace0724167695f8490b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7550"/><div sID="gen11688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7550"/><hi type="bold">33. The fear ... wisdom--</hi>Wisdom instructs in true piety.<div eID="gen11688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before ... humility--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Luke.24.26">Lu 24:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>); opposite (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.16.18">Pr 16:18</reference>). <chapter eID="Prov.15"/>

entries.22274562a10c052f64661dc3f1ec39e51f2d7e88: <div eID="gen24289" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24290" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24291" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24291" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24290" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24292" type="x-p"/> The soft answer. Useful correction. Stability of the righteous. The contented mind. The slothful man. The fool. The covetous. The impious. The wicked opposed to the righteous; to the diligent; and to the man who fears the Lord. <div eID="gen24292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24293" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24294" type="x-p"/> A soft answer - Gentleness will often disarm the most furious, where positive derangement has not taken place; one angry word will always beget another, for the disposition of one spirit always begets its own likeness in another: thus kindness produces kindness, and rage produces rage. Universal experience confirms this proverb.
entries.31deb49ec7dc0546db695f5dff27ee14f83a0e0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24295" type="x-p"/> Useth knowledge aright - This is very difficult to know: - when to speak, and when to be silent; what to speak, and what to leave unspoken; the manner that is best and most suitable to the occasion, the subject, the circumstances, and the persons. All these are difficulties, often even to the wisest men. Even wise counsel may be foolishly given.
entries.af3f7db5a42193dcc8eef60e0e6200c12968ea9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24296" type="x-p"/> The eyes of the Lord are in every place - He not only sees all things, by his omnipresence, but his providence is everywhere. And if the consideration that his eye is in every place, have a tendency to appal those whose hearts are not right before him, and who seek for privacy, that they may commit iniquity; yet the other consideration, that his providence is everywhere, has a great tendency to encourage the upright, and all who may be in perilous or distressing circumstances.
entries.c064ca27ebf89801b0449e2582f2a8cb5376a2f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24297" type="x-p"/> A wholesome tongue is a tree of life - Here again is an allusion to the paradisiacal tree, עץ חיים ets chaiyim, "the tree of lives."
entries.d428980341c1a51f67278e50fc370b34c480bd21: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24298" type="x-p"/> The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination - Even the most sedulous attendance on the ordinances of God, and pert ormance of the ceremonies of religion, is an abomination to the Lord, if the heart be not right with him, and the observance do not flow from a principle of pure devotion. No religious acts will do in place of holiness to the Lord. <div eID="gen24298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24299" type="x-p"/> The prayer of the upright is his delight - What a motive to be upright; and what a motive to the upright to pray! But who is the upright? The man who is weary of sin, and sincerely desires the salvation of God; as well as he who has already received a measure of that salvation. Hence it is said in the next verse, "He loveth him that followeth after righteousness."
entries.f22481dc98d7f4835b0dc56d44392bf0074576a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24300" type="x-p"/> Hell and destruction - שאול ואבדון sheol vaabaddon. Hades, the invisible world, the place of separate spirits till the resurrection: and Abaddon, the place of torment; are ever under the eye and control of the Lord.
entries.dfa55074d069f9a58e9d695a428891287a17dd4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24301" type="x-p"/> By sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken - Every kind of sorrow worketh death, but that which is the offspring of true repentance. This alone is healthful to the soul. The indulgence of a disposition to sighing tends to destroy life. Every deep sigh throws off a portion of the vital energy.
entries.9b24e60b88155f9b9a8a723b4c0922c6266394f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24302" type="x-p"/> Better is little with the fear of the Lord - Because where the fear of God is, there are moderation and contentment of spirit.
entries.48f2c494aa4ffcc2b3827e0f14ff9ca8d4d6ffef: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24303" type="x-p"/> Better is a dinner of herbs - Great numbers of indigent Hindoos subsist wholly on herbs, fried in oil, and mixed with their rice.
entries.ca47e4ae95c75363a0aa7cc9ca7b037526f08610: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24304" type="x-p"/> The way of the slothful man is as a hedge of thorns - Because he is slothful, he imagines ten thousand difficulties in the way which cannot be surmounted; but they are all the creatures of his own imagination, and that imagination is formed by his sloth.
entries.5b2bde306cf71fd866edead06acca9212867e626: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24305" type="x-p"/> But in the multitude of counsellors - See note on <reference osisRef="Pro.11.13">Pro 11:13</reference> (note). But רב יועצים rob yoatsim might be translated, chief or master of the council, the prime minister.
entries.66b93d59bfd95a55e25b3036e4d236afa3e98c85: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24306" type="x-p"/> The way of life is above to the wise - There is a treble antithesis here: <div eID="gen24306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24307" type="x-p"/> 1. The way of the wise, and that of the fool. <div eID="gen24307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24308" type="x-p"/> 2. The one is above, the other below. <div eID="gen24308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24309" type="x-p"/> 3. The one is of life, the other is of death.
entries.f7fae06b346a31138c6de8dca32c70e7871202b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24310" type="x-p"/> The house of the proud - Families of this description are seldom continued long. The Lord hates pride; and those that will not be humble he will destroy.
entries.a77f9e90f4d64d2d06ea28450e32a2d93fe4df23: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24311" type="x-p"/> He that is greedy of gain - He who will be rich; troubleth his own house - he is a torment to himself and his family by his avariciousness and penury, and a curse to those with whom he deals. <div eID="gen24311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24312" type="x-p"/> But he that hateth gifts - Whatever is given to pervert judgment.
entries.36bf516c4bf53bea02c09887b8c34eff8827d8d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen24312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24313" type="x-p"/> The heart of the righteous studieth to answer - His tongue never runs before his wit, he never speaks rashly, and never unadvisedly; because he studies - ponders, his thoughts and his words.
entries.e2f830d725c29452927b6d50b585a268e39ea5c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen24313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24314" type="x-p"/> The Lord is far from the wicked - He is neither near to hear, nor near to help.
entries.b0b78df610d453428229908d01011e888f5e86cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen24314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24315" type="x-p"/> The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart - Nature and art are continually placing before our view a multitude of the most resplendent images, each of which is calculated to give pleasure. The man who has a correct judgment, and an accurate eye, may not only amuse, but instruct himself endlessly, by the beauties of nature and art.
entries.97e83cced90a46ff688ba118dbbd5d8618762660: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen24315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24316" type="x-p"/> The ear that heareth the reproof - That receives it gratefully and obeys it. "Advice is for them that will take it," so says one of our own old proverbs; and the meaning here is nearly the same.
entries.bffee776b3255e44c86e68cbcb589e0dfb084f97: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen24316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24317" type="x-p"/> Despiseth his own soul - That is constructively; for if the instruction lead to the preservation of life and soul, he that neglects or despises it throws all as much in the way of danger as if he actually hated himself.
entries.e2dcd8a8aa826e7765e839186e93a3b11cb1c18f: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen24317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24318" type="x-p"/> The fear of the Lord - See note on <reference osisRef="Pro.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>. Much is spoken concerning this fear; <div eID="gen24318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24319" type="x-p"/> 1. It is the beginning of wisdom. <div eID="gen24319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24320" type="x-p"/> 2. It is also the beginning of knowledge. <div eID="gen24320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24321" type="x-p"/> 3. It is the instruction of wisdom. Wisdom derives its most important lessons from the fear of God. He who fears God much, is well taught. <div eID="gen24321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24322" type="x-p"/> And before honor is humility - That is, few persons ever arrive at honor who are not humble; and those who from low life have risen to places of trust and confidence, have been remarkable for humility. We may rest assured that the providence of God will never elevate a proud man; such God beholds afar off. He may get into places of trust and profit, but God will oust him, and the people will curse him, and curse his memory. So will it ever be with bad ministers and advisers of the crown.  <chapter eID="Prov.15"/> <div eID="gen24322" type="x-p"/>

entries.5fd4c1f198038efc1d0eacb42f187b1fefe4b5b9: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">Pro 15:1</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">1</reference> A soft answer turneth away wrath,    And a bitter word stirreth up anger. <div eID="gen11156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11157" type="x-p"/> In the second line, the common word for anger (אף, from the breathing with the nostrils, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.17">Pro 14:17</reference>) is purposely placed, but in the first, that which denotes anger in the highest degree (חמה from יחם, cogn. חמם, Arab. hamiya, to glow, like שׁנה from ישׁן): a mild, gentle word turns away the heat of anger (<hi type="italic">excandescentiam</hi>), puts it back, cf. Pro 25:15. The <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in רּך follows the rule of the דחיק, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of the close connection of a word terminating with the accented eh, aah, ah with the following word (<hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 63b). The same is the meaning of the Latin proverb:<hi type="italic">Frangitur ira gravis Quando est responsio suavis</hi>. <div eID="gen11157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11158" type="x-p"/> The דבר־עצב produces the contrary effect. This expression does not mean an angry word (Ewald), for עצב is not to be compared with the Arab. ghaḍab, anger (Umbreit), but with Arab. 'aḍb, cutting, wounding, paining (Hitzig), so that דבר מעציב is meant in the sense of <reference osisRef="Ps.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference> : a word which causes pain (lxx λυπηρός, Theod. πονικός), not after the meaning, a word provoking to anger (Gesenius), but certainly after its effect, for a wounding word “makes anger arise.” As one says of anger שׁב, “it turns itself” (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.11">Isa 9:11</reference>), so, on the other hand, עלה, “it rises up,” Ecc 10:4. The lxx has a third line, ὀργὴ ἀπόλλυσι καὶ φρονίμους, which the Syr. forms into a distich by the repetition of <reference osisRef="Prov.14.32">Pro 14:32</reference>, the untenableness of which is at once seen.
entries.aaefaf190df27d84b514b5e7797d91b1e68b8388: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.2">Pro 15:2</reference> <div eID="gen11158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11159" type="x-p"/> The πραΰ́της σοφίας (Jam 3:13) commended in <reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">Pro 15:1</reference> is here continued: <div eID="gen11159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11160" type="x-p"/> The tongue of the wise showeth great knowledge, <div eID="gen11160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11161" type="x-p"/> And the mouth of fools poureth forth folly. <div eID="gen11161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11162" type="x-p"/> As היטיב נגּן, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.16">Isa 23:16</reference>, means to strike the harp well, and היטיב לכת, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Isa 30:29</reference>, to go along merrily, so היטיב דּעת, to know in a masterly manner, and here, where the subject is the tongue, which has only an instrumental reference to knowledge: to bring to light great knowledge (cf. 7a). In 2b the lxx translate στόμα δὲ ἀφρόνων ἀναγγέλλει κακά. From this Hitzig concludes that they read רעות as 28b, and prefers this phrase; but they also translated in <reference osisRef="Prov.13.16">Pro 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.28">Pro 14:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.11">Pro 26:11</reference>, אוּלת by κακίαν, for they interpreted the unintelligible word by combination with עולת, and in <reference osisRef="Prov.12.23">Pro 12:23</reference> by ἀραῖς, for they thought they had before them אלות (from אלה).
entries.7d1b1437a051a0adc9cc86eb10d50be2589fc23c: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">Pro 15:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">3</reference> The eyes of Jahve are in every place,    Observing the evil and the good. <div eID="gen11162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11163" type="x-p"/> The connection of the <hi type="italic">dual</hi> עינים with the plur. of the adjective, which does not admit of a dual, is like <reference osisRef="Prov.6.17">Pro 6:17</reference>, cf. 18. But the first line is a sentence by itself, to which the second line gives a closer determination, as showing how the eyes of God are everywhere (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2Ch 16:9</reference>, after Zec 4:10) abroad over the whole earth, viz., beholding with penetrating look the evil and the good (צפה, to hold to, to observe, cf. ἐπιβλέποντες, Sir. 23:19), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, examining men whether they are good or evil, and keeping them closely before His eyes, so that nothing escapes him. This universal inspection, this omniscience of God, has an alarming but also a comforting side. The proverb seeks first to warn, therefore it speaks first of the evil.
entries.cfb9dfb111853bda08be9641a9bd38abcb907f63: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.4">Pro 15:4</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.4">4</reference> Gentleness of the tongue is a tree of life;    But falseness in it is a wounding to the spirit. <div eID="gen11163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11164" type="x-p"/> Regarding מרפּא, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.18">Pro 12:18</reference>, and regarding סלף, at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.3">Pro 11:3</reference>; this latter word we derive with Fleischer from סלף, to subvert, overthrow, but not in the sense of “violence, <hi type="italic">asperitas</hi>, in as far as violent speech is like a stormy sea,” but of perversity, perversitas (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. λοξότης), as the contrast to truthfulness, rectitude, kindness. Gentleness characterizes the tongue when all that it says to a neighbour, whether it be instruction or correction, or warning or consolation, it says in a manner without rudeness, violence, or obtrusiveness, by which it finds the easiest and surest acceptance, because he feels the goodwill, the hearty sympathy, the humility of him who is conscious of his own imperfection. Such gentleness is a tree of life, whose fruits preserve life, heal the sick, and raise up the bowed down. Accordingly, שׁבר בּרוּח is to be understood of the effect which goes forth from perversity or falseness of the tongue upon others. Fleischer translates: <hi type="italic">asperitas autem in ea animum vulnerat</hi>, and remarks, “שׁבר ברוח, <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concreto</hi>. The verb שׁבר, and the <hi type="italic">n. verbale</hi> שׁבר derived from it, may, in order to render the meaning tropical, govern the prep. בּ, as the Arab. kaser baḳlby, he has broken my heart (opp. Arab. jabar baḳlaby), cf. בּפניו, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.29">Pro 21:29</reference>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">De Glossis Habichtianis</hi>, p. 18; yet it also occurs with the accus., <reference osisRef="Ps.69.21">Psa 69:21</reference>, and the corresponding gen. שׁבר רוּח, Isa 65:14.” In any case, the breaking (deep wounding) is not meant in regard to his own spirit, but to that of the neighbour. Rightly Luther: but a lying (tongue) makes heart-sorrow (elsewhere, a false one troubles the cheerful); Euchel: a false tongue is soul-wounding; and the translation of the year 1844: falsehood is a breach into the heart. Only for curiosity’s sake are two other interpretations of 4a and 4b mentioned: the means of safety to the tongue is the tree of life, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, The <hi type="italic">Torâ</hi> (<hi type="italic">Erachin</hi> 15b); and: perversity suffers destruction by a breath of wind, after the proverb, כל שׁישׁ בו גסות רוח רוח קימעא שׁוברתו, a breath of wind breaks a man who is puffed up<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Duke’s <hi type="italic">Rabbinische Blumenlese</hi>, p. 176, where the rendering is somewhat different.</note> (which Meîri presents for choice, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., also Rashi, who understands רוח of the storm of judgment). The lxx translates, in 4b, a different text: ὁ δὲ συντηρῶν αὐτὴν πλησθήσεται πνεύματος; but the ישׂבּע רוּח here supposed cannot mean “to be full of spirit,” but rather “to eat full of wind.” Otherwise the Syr. and Targ.: and he who eateth of his own fruit is satisfied (Heb. ואכל מפּריו ישׂבּע) - an attempt to give to the phrase ישׂבע a thought correct in point of language, but one against which we do not give up the Masoretic text.
entries.d4bc7a4cbbb5f347390f74751d05b829c55a03a6: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.5">Pro 15:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.5">5</reference> A fool despiseth his father’s correction;    But he that regardeth reproof is prudent. <div eID="gen11164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11165" type="x-p"/> We may with equal correctness translate: he acts prudently (after <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.22">1Sa 23:22</reference>); and, he is prudent (after <reference osisRef="Prov.19.25">Pro 19:25</reference>). We prefer, with Jerome, <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther, the latter, against the lxx, Syr., and Targ., because, without a doubt, the יערם is so thought of at <reference osisRef="Prov.19.25">Pro 19:25</reference> : the contrast is more favourable to the former. It is true that he who regardeth reproof is not only prudent, but also that he is prudent by means of observing it. With line first cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.1.30">Pro 1:30</reference>, and with line second, Pro 12:1. Luther translates: the fool calumniates...; but of the meanings of abuse (properly <hi type="italic">pungere</hi>) and scorn, the second is perhaps here to be preferred.
entries.03b7f2be259224ce6b2eba55ad70cf55db1b76a0: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.6">Pro 15:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.6">6</reference> The house of the righteous is a great treasure-chamber;    But through the gain of the wicked comes trouble. <div eID="gen11165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11166" type="x-p"/> The contrast shows that חסן does not here mean force or might (lxx, Syr., Targ., Jerome, and <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.), which generally this derivative of the verb חסן never means, but store, fulness of possession, prosperity (Luther: in the house of the righteous are goods enough), in this sense (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Pro 27:24</reference>) placing itself, not with the Arab. ḥasuna, to be firm, fastened (Aram. ḥsn, חסן), but with Arab. khazan, to deposit, to lay up in granaries, whence our “<hi type="italic">Magazin</hi>.” חסן may indeed, like חיל, have the meaning of riches, and חסן does actually mean, in the Jewish-Aram., to possess, and the <hi type="italic">Aphel</hi> אחסן, to take into possession (κρατεῖν); but the constant use of the noun חסן in the sense of store, with the kindred idea of laying up, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.5">Jer 20:5</reference>, and of the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נחסן, which means, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa 23:18</reference>, with נאצר, “to be magazined,” gives countenance to the idea that חסן goes back to the primary conception, <hi type="italic">recondere</hi>, and is to be distinguished from חסון, חסין, and other derivatives after the fundamental conception. We may not interpret בּית, with Fleischer, Bertheau, and Zöckler, as accus.: in the house (cf. בּית, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.2">Pro 8:2</reference>), nor prepositionally as <hi type="italic">chez</hi> = <hi type="italic">casa</hi>; but: “the house of the righteous is a great store,” equivalent to, the place of such. On the contrary, destruction comes by the gain of the wicked. It is impossible that נעכּרת can have the house as the subject (Löwenstein), for בּית is everywhere mas. Therefore Abulwalîd, followed by Kimchi and the Venet. (ὄλεθρος), interprets נעכרת as subst., after the form of the Mishnic נברכת, a pool, cf. נחרצה, peremptorily decided, decreed; and if we do not extinguish the ב of וּבתבוּאת (the lxx according to the second translation of this doubly-translated distich, Syr., and Targ.), there remains then nothing further than to regard נעכרת either as subst. neut. overturned = overthrow (cf. such part. nouns as מוּסדה, מוּעקה, but particularly נסבּה, <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.15">2Ch 10:15</reference>), or as impers. neut. pass.: it is overthrown = there is an overthrow, like נשׂערה, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.3">Psa 50:3</reference> : it is stormed = a storm rages. The gain of the wicked has overthrow as its consequence, for the greed of gain, which does not shrink from unrighteous, deceitful gain, destroys his house, עכר בּיתו, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.27">Pro 15:27</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding עצר, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.29">Pro 11:29</reference>). Far from enriching the house, such gain is the cause of nothing but ruin. The lxx, in its first version of this distich, reads, in 6a, בּרבות צדק (ἐν πλεοναζούσῃ δικαιοσύνῃ), and in 6b, וּבתבוּאת רשׁע נעכּר (and together with the fruit the godless is rooted out, ὁλόῤῥιζοι ἐκ γῆς ἀπολοῦνται); for, as Lagarde has observed, it confounds עכר with עקר (to root, <hi type="italic">privativ</hi>: to root up). <div eID="gen11166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11167" type="x-p"/> A second series which begins with a proverb of the power of human speech, and closes with proverbs of the advantages and disadvantages of wealth.
entries.f07c49f415ed53eaf798135ea8f7e8bdc29fad4e: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.7">Pro 15:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.7">7</reference> The lips of the wise spread knowledge;    But the direction is wanting to the heart of fools. <div eID="gen11167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11168" type="x-p"/> It is impossible that לא־כן can be a second object. accus. dependent on יזרוּ (<hi type="italic">dispergunt</hi>, not יצּרוּ, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.28">Pro 20:28</reference>; φυλάσσουσι, as Symmachus translates): but the heart of fools is unrighteous (error or falsehood) (Hitzig after <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference>); for then why were the lips of the wise and the heart of the fools mentioned? לא־כן also does not mean οὐχ οὕτως (an old Greek anonymous translation, Jerome, Targ., <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., Luther): the heart of the fool is quite different from the heart of the wise man, which spreads abroad knowledge (Zöckler), for it is not heart and heart, but lip and heart, that are placed opposite to each other. Better the lxx οὐκ ἀσφαλεῖς, and yet better the Syr. lo kinı̂n (not right, sure). We have seen, at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.19">Pro 11:19</reference>, that כן as a participial adj. means standing = being, continuing, or also standing erect = right, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, rightly directed, or having the right direction; כּן־צדקה means there conducting oneself rightly, and thus genuine rectitude. What, after 7a, is more appropriate than to say of the heart of the fool, that it wants the receptivity for knowledge which the lips of the wise scatter abroad? The heart of the fool is not right, it has not the right direction, is crooked and perverse, has no mind for wisdom; and that which proceeds from the wise, therefore, finds with him neither estimation nor acceptance.
entries.8cc59e32f859b873896a85d5da70cca4be325aa8: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">Pro 15:8</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.8">8</reference> The sacrifice of the godless is an abhorrence to Jahve;    But the prayer of the upright is His delight. <div eID="gen11168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11169" type="x-p"/> Although the same is true of the prayer of the godless that is here said of their sacrifice, and of the sacrifice of the righteous that is here said of their prayer (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Pro 28:9</reference>, and cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.27.6">Psa 27:6</reference>), yet it is not by accident that here (line first = <reference osisRef="Prov.21.27">Pro 21:27</reference>) the sacrifice is ascribed to the godless and the prayer to the upright. The sacrifice, as a material and legally-required performance, is much more related to dead works than prayer freely completing itself in the word, the most direct expression of the personality, which, although not commanded by the law, because natural to men, as such is yet the soul of all sacrifices; and the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, like the Psalms and Prophets, in view of the ceremonial service which had become formal and dead in the <hi type="italic">opus operatum</hi>, is to such a degree penetrated by the knowledge of the incongruity of the offering up of animals and of plants, with the object in view, that a proverb like “the sacrifice of the righteous is pleasing to God” never anywhere occurs; and if it did occur without being expressly and unavoidably referred to the legal sacrifice, it would have to be understood rather after Psa 51:18. than Ps. 51:20f., rather after <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference> than after <reference osisRef="Ps.66.13">Psa 66:13</reference>-15. זבח, which, when it is distinguished from עולה, means (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.7.14">Pro 7:14</reference>) the sacrifice only in part coming to the altar, for the most part applied to a sacrificial feast, is here the common name for the bloody, and, <hi type="italic">per synecdochen</hi>, generally the legally-appointed sacrifice, consisting in external offering. The לרצין, <reference osisRef="Lev.1.3">Lev 1:3</reference>, used in the <hi type="italic">Tôra</hi> of sacrifices, is here, as at Ps. 19:15, transferred to prayer. The fundamental idea of the proverb is, that sacrifices well-pleasing to God, prayers acceptable to God (that are heard, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.29">Pro 15:29</reference>), depend on the relations in which the heart and life of the man stand to God.
entries.80be6f82b54d641c4e9385fbb80455312b294231: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.9">Pro 15:9</reference> <div eID="gen11169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11170" type="x-p"/> Another proverb with the key-word תועבת <div eID="gen11170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11171" type="x-p"/> An abomination to Jahve is the way of the godless; <div eID="gen11171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11172" type="x-p"/> But He loveth him who searcheth after righteousness. <div eID="gen11172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11173" type="x-p"/> The manner and rule of life is called the way. מרדּף is the heightening of רדף, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.21">Pro 21:21</reference>, and can be used independently <hi type="italic">in bonam</hi>, as well as <hi type="italic">in malam partem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.19">Pro 11:19</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.13.21">Pro 13:21</reference>). Regarding the form יאהב, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer in <hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitsch</hi>. xv. 382.
entries.f6a0b6edc18775e135014625e557103b4bc1205c: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.10">Pro 15:10</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.10">10</reference> Sharp correction is for him who forsaketh the way;      Whoever hateth instruction shall die. <div eID="gen11173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11174" type="x-p"/> The way, thus absolute, is the God-pleasing right way (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.13">Pro 2:13</reference>), the forsaking of which is visited with the punishment of death, because it is that which leadeth unto life (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.17">Pro 10:17</reference>). And that which comes upon them who leave it is called מוּסר רע, <hi type="italic">castigatio dura</hi>, as much as to say that whoever does not welcome instruction, whoever rejects it, must at last receive it against his will in the form of peremptory punishment. The sharp correction (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.28.28">Isa 28:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.19">Isa 28:19</reference>) is just the death under which he falls who accepts of no instruction (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.23">Pro 5:23</reference>), temporal death, but that as a token of wrath which it is not for the righteous (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.32">Pro 14:32</reference>).
entries.12268809606be583b73e814fbc43d29097138d33: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.11">Pro 15:11</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.11">11</reference> The underworld [Sheol] and the abyss are before Jahve;      But how much more the hearts of the children of men! <div eID="gen11174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11175" type="x-p"/> A syllogism, <hi type="italic">a minori ad majus</hi>, with אף כּי (lxx τῶς οὐχὶ καὶ, <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. μᾶλλον οὖν), like 12:32.<note placement="foot">In Rabbin. this concluding form is called קל וחמר (light and heavy over against one another), and דּין (judgment, viz., from <hi type="italic">premisses</hi>, thus conclusion), κατ ̓ ἐξ. Instead of the biblical אף כי, the latter form of the language has כּל־שׁכּן (all speaks for it that it is so), על־אחת כּמּה וכמּה (so much the more), אינו דּין, or also קל וחמר (as <hi type="italic">minori ad majus</hi> = <hi type="italic">quanto magis</hi>); <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the <hi type="italic">Hebr. Römerbrief</hi>, p. 14.</note> אבדּון has a meaning analogous to that of τάρταρος (cf. ταρταροῦν, 2Pe 2:4, to throw down into the τάρταρος), which denotes the lowest region of Hades (שׁאול תּחתּית or תּחתּיּה 'שׁ), and also in general, Hades. If אבדון and מות are connected, <reference osisRef="Job.37.22">Job 37:22</reference>, and if אבדון is the parallel word to קבר, <reference osisRef="Ps.88.12">Psa 88:12</reference>, or also to שׁאול, as in the passage similar to this proverb, <reference osisRef="Job.26.6">Job 26:6</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.38.17">Job 38:17</reference>): “Sheôl is naked before Him, and Abaddon has no covering;” since אבדון is the general name of the underworld, including the grave, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the inner place of the earth which receives the body of the dead, as the kingdom of the dead, lying deeper, does the soul. But where, as here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.27.10">Pro 27:10</reference>, שׁאול and אבדון stand together, they are related to each other, as ᾅδης and ταρταρος or ἅβυσσος, <reference osisRef="Rev.9.11">Rev 9:11</reference> : אבדון is the lowest hell, the place of deepest descent, of uttermost destruction. The conclusion which is drawn in the proverb proceeds from the supposition that in the region of creation there is nothing more separated, and by a wide distance, from God, than the depth, and especially the undermost depth, of the realm of the dead. If now God has this region in its whole compass wide open before Him, if it is visible and thoroughly cognisable by Him (נגד, <hi type="italic">acc. adv.: in conspectu</hi>, from נגד, <hi type="italic">eminere, conspicuum esse</hi>) - for He is also present in the underworld, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference> - then much more will the hearts of the children of men be open, the inward thoughts of men living and acting on the earth being known already from their expressions. Man sees through man, and also himself, never perfectly; but the Lord can try the heart and prove the reins, Jer 17:10. What that means this proverb gives us to understand, for it places over against the hearts of men nothing less than the depths of the underworld in eternity.
entries.4fe97dada45ac5b796f04bbae15153726a338e87: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.12">Pro 15:12</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.12">12</reference> The scorner liketh not that one reprove him,      To wise men he will not go. <div eID="gen11175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11176" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <hi type="italic">absol</hi>., abruptly denoting the action, may take the place of the object, as here (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.9.18">Job 9:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.24">Isa 42:24</reference>), as well as of the subject (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.27">Pro 25:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.6.25">Job 6:25</reference>). Thus הוכיח is (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.7">Pro 9:7</reference>) construed with the dat. obj. Regarding the probable conclusion which presents itself from passages such as <reference osisRef="Prov.15.12">Pro 15:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.13.20">Pro 13:20</reference>, as to the study of wisdom in Israel, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 39. Instead of אל, we read, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.20">Pro 13:20</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.24">Pro 22:24</reference>), את־; for לכת את־ means to have intercourse with one, to go a journey with one (Mal 2:6, cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.5.24">Gen 5:24</reference>, but not <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.22">2Sa 15:22</reference>, where we are to translate with Keil), according to which the lxx has here μετὰ δὲ σοφῶν οὐχ ὁμιλήσει. The mocker of religion and of virtue shuns the circle of the wise, for he loves not to have his treatment of that which is holy reproved, nor to be convicted of his sin against truth; he prefers the society where his frivolity finds approbation and a response.
entries.594660b18ca1bd68410db84a9709bf0cfaf6cf1b: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.13">Pro 15:13</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.13">13</reference> A joyful heart maketh the countenance cheerful;      But in sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken. <div eID="gen11176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11177" type="x-p"/> The expression of the countenance, as well as the spiritual <hi type="italic">habitus</hi> of a man, is conditioned by the state of the heart. A joyful heart maketh the countenance טוב, which means friendly, but here happy-looking = cheerful (for טוב ro is the most general designation of that which makes an impression which is pleasant to the senses or to the mind); on the contrary, with sorrow of heart (עצּבת, constr. of עצּבת, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.10">Pro 10:10</reference>, as חטאת = חטּאת, from חטּאה) there is connected a stricken, broken, downcast heart; the spiritual functions of the man are paralyzed; self-confidence, without which energetic action is impossible, is shattered; he appears discouraged, whereby רוּח is thought of as the power of self-consciousness and of self-determination, but לב, as our “<hi type="italic">Gemüt</hi>” [<hi type="italic">animus</hi>], as the oneness of thinking and willing, and thus as the seat of determination, which decides the intellectual-corporeal life-expression of the man, or without being able to be wholly restrained, communicates itself to them. The ב of וּבעצּבת is, as Pro 15:16., <reference osisRef="Prov.16.8">Pro 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.1">Pro 17:1</reference>, meant in the force of being together or along with, so that רוּח נכאה do not need to be taken separate from each other as subject and predicate: the sense of the noun-clause is in the ב, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, also <reference osisRef="Prov.7.23">Pro 7:23</reference> (it is about his life, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it concerns his life). Elsewhere the crushed spirit, like the broken heart, is equivalent to the heart despairing in itself and prepared for grace. The heart with a more clouded mien may be well, for sorrow has in it a healing power (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.3">Ecc 7:3</reference>). But here the matter is the general psychological truth, that the corporeal and spiritual life of man has its regulator in the heart, and that the condition of the heart leaves its stamp on the appearance and on the activity of the man. The translation of the רוח נכאה by “oppressed breath” (Umbreit, Hitzig) is impossible; the breath cannot be spoken of as broken.
entries.377815404be770b7bc158a8fc4e5ee6261ed3ebd: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.14">Pro 15:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.14">14</reference> The heart of the understanding seeketh after knowledge,      And the mouth of fools practiseth folly. <div eID="gen11177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11178" type="x-p"/> Luther interprets רעה as metaphor. for to govern, but with such ethical conceptions it is metaphor. for to be urgently circumspect about anything (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.13.20">Pro 13:20</reference>), like Arab. ra'y and r'âyt, intentional, careful, concern about anything. No right translation can be made of the Chethib פני, which Schultens, Hitzig, Ewald, and Zöckler prefer; the predicate can go before the פּני, after the Semitic rule in the fem. of the sing., <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.9">2Sa 10:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.16.16">Job 16:16</reference>, Chethib, but cannot follow in the masc. of the sing.; besides, the operations of his look and aspect are ascribed to his face, but not spiritual functions as here, much more to the mouth, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to the spirit speaking through it. The heart is within a man, and the mouth without; and while the former gives and takes, the latter is always only giving out. In <reference osisRef="Prov.18.15">Pro 18:15</reference>, where a synonymous distich is formed from the antithetic distich, the ear, as hearing, is mentioned along with the heart as appropriating. נבון is not an adj., but is gen., like צדיק, 28a (opp. ופי). חכם, Pro 16:23. The φιλοσοφία of the understanding is placed over against the μωρολογία of the fools. The lxx translates καρδία ὀρθὴ ζητεῖ αἲσθησιν (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.14.10">Pro 14:10</reference>, καρδία ἀδρὸς αἰσθητική); it uses this word after the Hellenistic <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>. for דעת, of experimental knowledge.
entries.85fa044537c09370b51bbeac0a86385e731e1009: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.15">Pro 15:15</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.15">15</reference> All the days of the afflicted are evil;      But he who is of a joyful heart hath a perpetual feast. <div eID="gen11178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11179" type="x-p"/> Regarding עני (the afflicted), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., 21b. They are so called on whom a misfortune, or several of them, press externally or internally. If such an one is surrounded by ever so many blessings, yet is his life day by day a sad one, because with each new day the feeling of his woe which oppresses him renews itself; whoever, on the contrary, is of joyful heart (gen. connection as <reference osisRef="Prov.11.13">Pro 11:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.8">Pro 12:8</reference>), such an one (his life) is always a feast, a banquet (not משׁתּה, as it may be also pointed, but משׁתּה and תּמיד thus <hi type="italic">adv</hi>., for it is never adj.; the post-bib. usage is תּמידין for עולות תּמיד). Hitzig (and also Zöckler) renders 15b: And (the days) of one who is of a joyful heart are.... Others supply לו (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.27.7">Pro 27:7</reference>), but our rendering does not need that. We have here again an example of that attribution (Arab. isnâd) in which that which is attributed (musnad) is a condition (hal) of a logical subject (the musnad ilêhi), and thus he who speaks has this, not in itself, but in the sense of the condition; the inwardly cheerful is feasts evermore, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the condition of such an one is like a continual festival. The true and real happiness of a man is thus defined, not by external things, but by the state of the heart, in which, in spite of the apparently prosperous condition, a secret sorrow may gnaw, and which, in spite of an externally sorrowful state, may be at peace, and be joyfully confident in God.
entries.de5ba64bf0ce379ed6922df4d69c83a3f53a5af1: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.16">Pro 15:16</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.16">16</reference> Better is little with the fear of Jahve,      Than great store and trouble therewith. <div eID="gen11179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11180" type="x-p"/> The ב in both cases the lxx rightly renders by μετά. How מהוּמה (elsewhere of wild, confused disorder, extreme discord) is meant of store and treasure, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.7">Psa 39:7</reference> shows: it is restless, covetous care and trouble, as the contrast of the quietness and contentment proceeding from the fear of God, the noisy, wild, stormy running and hunting about of the slave of mammon. Theodotion translates the word here, as Aquila and Symmachus elsewhere, by words which correspond (φαγέδαινα = φάγαινα or ἀχορτασία) with the Syr. יענותא, greed or insatiability.
entries.9968aaf32caa50679908b89a6ee979b44c6b300d: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.17">Pro 15:17</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.17">17</reference> Better a dish of cabbage, and love with it,      Than a fatted ox together with hatred. <div eID="gen11180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11181" type="x-p"/> With בו is here interchanged שׁם, which, used both of things and of persons, means to be there along with something. Both have the <hi type="italic">Dag. forte conj</hi>., cf. to the contrary, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.20">Deu 30:20</reference>; Mic 1:11; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.22">Deu 11:22</reference>; the punctuation varies, if the first of the two words is a <hi type="italic">n. actionis</hi> ending in  ה. The dish (portion) is called ארחה, which the lxx and other Greek versions render by ξενισμός, entertainment, and thus understand it of that which is set before a guest, perhaps rightly so, for the Arab. ârrakh (to date, to determine), to which it is compared by Gesenius and Dietrich, is equivalent to warrh, a denom. of the name of the moon. Love and hatred are, according to circumstances, the disposition of the host, or of the participant, the spirit of the family:<hi type="italic">Cum dat oluscula mensa minuscula pace quietâ</hi>,<hi type="italic">Ne pete grandia lautaque prandia lite repleta</hi>.
entries.1d217c55a6d3c3798f635f8c3ac2b38465b4a284: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.18">Pro 15:18</reference> <div eID="gen11181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11182" type="x-p"/> Two proverbs of two different classes of men, each second line of which terminates with a catchword having a similar sound (וארך, וארח). 18 A passionate man stirreth up strife,      And one who is slow to anger allayeth contention. <div eID="gen11182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11183" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.25">Pro 28:25</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.29.22">Pro 29:22</reference> are variations of the first line of this proverb. The <hi type="italic">Pih</hi>. גּרה occurs only these three times in the phrase גּרה מדון, R. גר, to grind, thus to strike, to irritate, cogn. to (but of a different root from) the verb עורר, to excite, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pro 10:12</reference>, and חרחר, to set on fire, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.21">Pro 26:21</reference>, cf. שׁלּח, Pro 6:14. Regarding חמה, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">Pro 15:1</reference>; we call such a man a “hot-head;” but the biblical conception nowhere (except in the Book of Daniel) places the head in connection with spiritual-psychical events (<hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 254). Regarding ארך אפּים, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.14.29">Pro 14:29</reference>; the lxx (which contains a translation of this proverb, and after it of a variation) translates μακρόθυμος δὲ καὶ τὴν μέλλουσαν καταπρᾳύνει, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, (as the Syr. render it) he suppresses the strife in its origin, so that it does not break out. But both are true: that he who is slow to anger, who does not thus easily permit himself to become angry, allayeth the strife which one enters into with him, or into which he is drawn, and that he prevents the strife, for he places over against provoking, injurious conduct, patient gentleness (מרפּא, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4">Ecc 10:4</reference>).
entries.6134d7f805f08276a7b79b5dbc200da028ef17ab: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.19">Pro 15:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.19">19</reference> The way of the slothful is as hedged with thorns;      But the path of the righteous is paved. <div eID="gen11183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11184" type="x-p"/> Hitzig misses the contrast between אצל (slothful) and ישׁרים (upright), and instead of the slothful reads עריץ, the tyrannical. But is then the slothful ישׁר? The contrast is indeed not that of contradiction, but the slothful is one who does not act uprightly, a man who fails to fulfil the duty of labour common to man, and of his own special calling. The way of such an one is כּמשׂכת חדק, like a fencing with thorns (from חדק, R. חד, to be pointed, sharp, distinguished from Arab. hadḳ, to surround, and in the meaning to fix with the look, denom. of khadaḳt, the apple of the eye), so that he goes not forwards, and sees hindrances and difficulties everywhere, which frighten him back, excusing his shunning his work, his remissness of will, and his doing nothing; on the contrary, the path of those who wait truly and honestly on their calling, and prosecute their aim, is raised up like a skilfully made street, so that unhindered and quickly they go forward (סלוּלה, R. סל, <hi type="italic">aggerare</hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">Jer 18:15</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.49.11">Isa 49:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Isa 49:4</reference> :<reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">8</reference>, סלסל, which was still in use in the common language of Palestine in the second cent., <hi type="italic">Rosch haschana</hi>, 26b).
entries.7958bd2647b813f8179fc4e43ec95449588fc659: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.20-Prov.15.23">Pro 15:20-23</reference> <div eID="gen11184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11185" type="x-p"/> This collection of Solomonic proverbs began, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">Pro 10:1</reference>, with a proverb having reference to the observance of the fourth commandment,<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">fifth</hi> commandment of the Westminster Shorter Catechism is named as the <hi type="italic">fourth</hi> in Luther’s catechism.</note> and a second chief section, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.1">Pro 13:1</reference>, began in the same way. Here a proverb of the same kind designates the beginning of a third chief section. That the editor was aware of this is shown by the homogeneity of the proverbs, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.19">Pro 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.28">Pro 12:28</reference>, which form the conclusion of the first and second sections. We place together first in this new section, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.20-Prov.15.23">Pro 15:20-23</reference>, in which (with the exception of <reference osisRef="Prov.15.25">Pro 15:25</reference>) the ישׂמח [maketh glad] of the first (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">Pro 10:1</reference>) is continued.  <reference osisRef="Prov.15.20">Pro 15:20</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.20">20</reference> A wise son maketh a glad father,      And a fool of a man despiseth his mother. <div eID="gen11185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11186" type="x-p"/> Line first = Pro 10:1. The gen. connection of כּסיל אדם (here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.21.20">Pro 21:20</reference>) is not superlative the most foolish of men, but like פּרא אדם, <reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Gen 16:12</reference>; the latter: a man of the wild ass kind; the former: a man of the fool kind, who is the exemplar of such a sort among men. Piety acting in willing subordination is wisdom, and the contrary exceeding folly.
entries.e50eae7c24c4c8e779408c855d578589eefee961: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.24">Pro 15:24</reference> <div eID="gen11189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11190" type="x-p"/> Four proverbs of fundamentally different doctrines: 24 The man of understanding goeth upwards on a way of life,      To depart from hell beneath. <div eID="gen11190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11191" type="x-p"/> The way of life is one, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.6">Pro 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference> (where, notwithstanding the want of the article, the idea is logically determined), although in itself forming a plurality of ארחות, Pro 2:19. “A way of life,” in the translation, is equivalent to a way which is a way of life. למעלה, upwards (as <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.21">Ecc 3:21</reference>, where, in the doubtful question whether the spirit of a man at his death goes upwards, there yet lies the knowledge of the alternative), belongs, as the parallel משּׁאול מטּה shows, to ארח חיּים as virtual adj.: a way of life which leads upwards. And the ל of למשׂכּיל is that of possession, but not as of quiet possession (such belongs to him), but as personal activity, as in דּרך לו, he has a journey = he makes a journey, finds himself on a journey, 1Ki 18:27; for למען סוּר is not merely, as לסוּר, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.14">Pro 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.27">Pro 14:27</reference>, the expression of the end and consequence, but of the subjective object, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the intention, and thus supposes an activity corresponding to this intention. The O.T. reveals heaven, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the state of the revelation of God in glory, yet not as the abode of saved men; the way of the dying leads, according to the O.T. representation, downwards into Sheôl; but the translations of Enoch and Elijah are facts which, establishing the possibility of an exception, break through the dark monotony of that representation, and, as among the Greeks the mysteries encouraged ἡδυστέρας ἐλπίδας, so in Israel the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> appears pointing the possessor of wisdom upwards, and begins to shed light on the darkness of Sheôl by the new great thoughts of a life of immortality, thus of a ζωὴ αἰώνιος (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.28">Pro 12:28</reference>) (<hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 407ff.), now for the first time becoming prominent, but only as a foreboding and an enigma. The idea of the Sheôl opens the way for a change: the gathering place of all the living on this side begins to be the place of punishment for the godless (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.27">Pro 7:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference>); the way leading upwards, εἰς τὴν ζωὴν, and that leading downwards, εἰς τὴν ἀπωλειαν (Mat 7:13.), come into direct contrast.
entries.3229261f044be24122b93274de731f79a9ce9179: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.25">Pro 15:25</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.25">25</reference> The house of the proud Jahve rooteth out,      And He establisheth the landmark of the widow. <div eID="gen11191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11192" type="x-p"/> The power unnamed in יסּחוּ, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.22">Pro 2:22</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.14.11">Pro 14:11</reference>), is here named יסּח יהוה (thus to be pointed with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> following). יצּב is the abbreviated fut. form which the elevated style, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.8">Deu 32:8</reference>, uses also as indic. - a syntactical circumstance which renders Hitzig’s correction ויּצּב superfluous. It is the border of the land-possession of the widows, removed by the גּאים (lxx ὑβριστῶν), that is here meant. The possession of land in Israel was secured by severe punishment inflicted in him who removed the “landmark” (<reference osisRef="Deut.19.14">Deu 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.27.17">Deu 27:17</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.28">Pro 22:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.2">Pro 24:2</reference>) as well as the prophets (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Hos 5:10) inculcate the inviolability of the borders of the possession, as the guardian of which Jahve here Himself appears.
entries.634644665418097df277c88359fe2e75c05a5930: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.26">Pro 15:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.26">26</reference> An abomination to Jahve are evil thoughts;      But gracious words are to Him pure. <div eID="gen11192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11193" type="x-p"/> Not personally (Luther: the plans of the wicked) but neutrally is רע here meant as at <reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">Pro 2:14</reference>, and in אושׁת רע, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.24">Pro 6:24</reference> (cf. Pers. merdi nı̂ku, man of good = good man), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Friedr. Philippi’s <hi type="italic">Status Constr</hi>. p. 121. Thoughts which are of a bad kind and of a bad tendency, particularly (what the parallel member brings near) of a bad disposition and design against others, are an abomination to God; but, on the contrary, pure, viz., in His eyes, which cannot look upon iniquity (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Hab 1:13</reference>), are the אמרי־נעם, words of compassion and of friendship toward men, which are (after 26a) the expression of such thoughts, thus sincere, benevolent words, the influence of which on the soul and body of him to whom they refer is described, Pro 16:24. The Syr., Targ., Symmachus, Theodotion, and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. recognise in וּטהורים the pred., while, on the contrary, the lxx, Jerome, and Luther (who finally decided for the translation, “but the pure speak comfortably”) regard it as subject. But that would be an attribution which exceeds the measure of possibility, and for which אמרים or דברי must be used; also the parallelism requires that טהורים correspond with 'תועבת ה. Hence also the reference of וטהורים to the judgment of God, which is determined after the motive of pure untainted law; that which proceeds from such, that and that only, is pure, pure in His sight, and thus also pure in itself.
entries.21dd9d4aaed573ae5d7e67db4ee9361f64a55ef5: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.27">Pro 15:27</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.27">27</reference> Whoever does service to [<hi type="italic">servit</hi>] avarice troubleth his own house;      But he that hateth gifts shall live. <div eID="gen11193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11194" type="x-p"/> Regarding בּצע בּצע, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.19">Pro 1:19</reference>, and regarding עכר בּיתו, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.29">Pro 11:29</reference>, where it is subject, but here object.; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.16">Pro 28:16</reference> is a variation of 27b. מתּנות are here gifts in the sense of <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Ecc 7:7</reference>, which pervert judgment, and cause respect of persons. The lxx from this point mingles together a series of proverbs with those of the following chapter.
entries.d4828b56c8031671852b6305e7b9c678add29dec: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.28">Pro 15:28</reference> <div eID="gen11194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11195" type="x-p"/> Two proverbs regarding the righteous and the wicked: 28 The heart of the righteous considereth how to answer right,      And the mouth of the godless poureth forth evil. <div eID="gen11195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11196" type="x-p"/> Instead of לענות, the lxx (Syr. and Targ.) imagines אמוּנות πίστεις; Jerome translates, but falsely, <hi type="italic">obedientiam</hi> (from ענה, to bend oneself); Meîri thinks on לענה, wormwood, for the heart of the righteous revolves in itself the misery and the vanity of this present life; Hitzig corrects this verse as he does the three preceding: the heart of the righteous thinks on ענוות, a plur. of verb ענוה, which, except in this correction, does not exist. The proverb, as it stands, is, in fineness of expression and sharpness of the contrast, raised above such manglings. Instead of the righteous, the wise might be named, and instead of the godless, fools (cf. 2b); but the poet places the proverb here under the point of view of duty to neighbours. It is the characteristic of the righteous that he does not give the reins to his tongue; but as Luther has translated: the heart of the righteous considers [<hi type="italic">tichtet</hi> from <hi type="italic">dictare</hi>, frequently to speak, here carefully to think over] what is to be answered, or rather, since מה־לּענות is not used, he thinks thereupon to answer rightly, for that the word ענות is used in this pregnant sense is seen from 23a. The godless, on the contrary, are just as rash with their mouth as the righteous are of a thoughtful heart: their mouth sputters forth (<hi type="italic">effutit</hi>) evil, for they do not first lay to heart the question what may be right and just in the case that has arisen.
entries.1cd1631ce6d333db705330cd37138e792814b446: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.29">Pro 15:29</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.29">29</reference> Jahve is far from the godless;      But the prayer of the righteous He heareth. <div eID="gen11196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11197" type="x-p"/> Line second is a variation of 8b. God is far from the godless, viz., as Polychronius remarks, <hi type="italic">non spatii intercapedine, sed sententiae diversitate</hi>; more correctly: as to His gracious presence - חלץ מהם, He has withdrawn Himself from them, Hos 10:6, so that if they pray, their prayer reaches not to Him. The prayer of the righteous, on the contrary, He hears, He is graciously near to them, they have access to Him, He listens to their petitions; and if they are not always fulfilled according to their word, yet they are not without an answer (<reference osisRef="Ps.145.18">Psa 145:18</reference>).
entries.5fbdaea707bfdfbafec62041d9e6ef0b4fd90458: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.30">Pro 15:30</reference> <div eID="gen11197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11198" type="x-p"/> Two proverbs regarding the eye and the ear: 30 The light of the eye rejoiceth the heart,      And a good message maketh the bones fat. <div eID="gen11198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11199" type="x-p"/> Hitzig corrects also here: מראה עינים, that which is seen with the eyes, viz., after long desire; and certainly מראה עינים can mean not only that which the eyes see (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.3">Isa 11:3</reference>), but also this, that the eyes do see. But is it true what Hitzig says in justification of his correction, that מאור never means light, or ray, or brightness, but lamp (φωστήρ)? It is true, indeed, that מאור עינים cannot mean a cheerful sight (Luther) in an objective sense (lxx θεωρῶνὀφθαλμὸς καλά), as a verdant garden or a stream flowing through a landscape (Rashi), for that would be מראה מאיר עינים, and “brightness which the eyes see” (Bertheau); the genitive connection certainly does not mean: the מאור is not the light from without presenting itself to the eyes, but, like אור עינים (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.11">Psa 38:11</reference>) and similar expressions, the light of the eye itself [bright or joyous eyes]. But מאור does not mean alone the body of light, but also the illumination, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.14">Exo 35:14</reference> and elsewhere, not only that which (ὄ, τι) gives light, but also this, that (ὄτι) light arises and is present, so that we might translate it here as at <reference osisRef="Ps.90.8">Psa 90:8</reference>, either the brightness, or that which gives light. But the clear brightness of one’s own eye cannot be meant, for then that were as much as to say that it is the effect, not that it is the cause, of a happy heart, but the brightness of the eyes of others that meet us. That this gladdens the heart of him who has a sight of it is evident, without any interchanging relation of the joy-beaming countenance, for it is indeed heart-gladdening to a man, to whom selfishness has not made the χαίρειν μετὰ χαιρόντων impossible, to see a countenance right joyful in truth. But in connection with <reference osisRef="Prov.16.15">Pro 16:15</reference>, it lies nearer to think on a love-beaming countenance, a countenance on which joyful love to us mirrors itself, and which reflects itself in our heart, communicating this sense of gladness. The ancient Jewish interpreters understand מאור עינים of the enlightening of the eye of the mind, according to which Euchel translates: “clear intelligence;” but Rashi has remarked that that is not the explanation of the words, but the Midrash. That, in line second of this synonymous distich, שׁמוּעה טובה does not mean <hi type="italic">alloquium humanum</hi> (Fl.), nor a good report which one hears of himself, but a good message, is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Prov.25.25">Pro 25:25</reference>; שׁמוּעה as neut. <hi type="italic">part. pass</hi>. may mean that which is heard, but the comparison of ישׁוּעה, שׁבוּעה, stamps it as an abstract formation like גּאלּה, גּדלּה (גּדוּלה), according to which the lxx translates it by ἀκοή (in this passage by φήμη). Regarding דּשּׁן, richly to satisfy, or to refresh, a favourite expression in the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.25">Pro 11:25</reference>; Pro 13:4.
entries.0738cc4ae9cc84c7e84b715e489338a945a1b5f2: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.31">Pro 15:31</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.31">31</reference> An ear which heareth the doctrine of life      Keeps itself in the circle of the wise. <div eID="gen11199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11200" type="x-p"/> As, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.33">Pro 6:33</reference>, תוכחות מוסר means instructions aiming at discipline, so here תּוכחת חיּים means instructions which have life as their end, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as showing how one may attain unto true life; Hitzig’s חכם, for חיים, is a fancy. Is now the meaning this, that the ear which willingly hears and receives such doctrine of life will come to dwell among the wise, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, that such an one (for אזן is <hi type="italic">synecdoche partis pro persona</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Job.29.11">Job 29:11</reference>) will have his residence among wise men, as being one of them, <hi type="italic">inter eos sedem firmam habebit iisque annumerabitur</hi> (Fl.)? By such a rendering, one is surprised at the harshness of the synecdoche, as well as at the circumstantiality of the expression (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.13.20">Pro 13:20</reference>, יחכּם). On the contrary, this corresponds with the thought that one who willingly permits to be said to him what he must do and suffer in order that he may be a partaker of life, on this account remains most gladly in the circle of the wise, and there has his appropriate place. The “passing the night” (לין, cogn. ליל, Syr. Targ. בּוּת, Arab. bât) is also frequently elsewhere the designation of prolonged stay, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Isa 1:21. בּקרב is here different in signification from that it had in <reference osisRef="Prov.14.23">Pro 14:23</reference>, where it meant “in the heart.” In the lxx this proverb is wanting. The other Greek translations have οὖς ἀκοῦον ἐλέγχους χωῆς ἐν μέσῳ σοφῶν αὐλισθήσεται. Similarly the Syr., Targ., Jerome, <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther, admitting both renderings, but, since they render in the fut., bringing nearer the idea of prediction (Midrash: זוכה לישׁב בישׁיבת חכמים) than of description of character.
entries.27a8f29936e537ccf70b3147bf159a814e1baff7: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.32">Pro 15:32</reference> <div eID="gen11200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11201" type="x-p"/> Two proverbs with the catchword מוּסר: 32 He that refuseth correction lightly values his soul;      But he that heareth reproof getteth understanding. <div eID="gen11201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11202" type="x-p"/> Regarding פּורע מוּסר, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.13.18">Pro 13:18</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.25">Pro 1:25</reference>, and מואס נפשׁו, Pro 8:36. נפשׁו contains more than the later expression עצמו, self; it is equivalent to חיּיו (<reference osisRef="Job.9.21">Job 9:21</reference>), for the נפשׁ is the bond of union between the intellectual and the corporeal life. The despising of the soul is then the neglecting, endangering, exposing of the life; in a word, it is suicide (10b). <reference osisRef="Prov.19.8">Pro 19:8</reference> is a variation derived from this distich: “He who gains understanding loves his soul,” according to which the lxx translate here ἀγαπᾷ ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ. לב the Midrash explains by חכמה שׁנתונה בלב; but the correct view is, that לב is not thought of as a formal power, but as operative and carried into effect in conformity with its destination.
entries.7d57a26229dcb639a847bc41d66bc558310e20c8: <reference osisRef="Prov.15.33">Pro 15:33</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.33">33</reference> The fear of Jahve is a discipline to wisdom,      And before honour is humility. <div eID="gen11202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11203" type="x-p"/> We may regard 'יראת ה (the fear of Jahve) also as pred. here. The fear of Jahve is an educational maxim, and the end of education of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>; but the phrase may also be the subject, and by such a rendering Luther’s parallelism lies nearer: “The fear of the Lord is discipline to wisdom;” the fear of God, viz., continually exercised and tried, is the right school of wisdom, and humility is the right way to honour. Similar is the connection מוּסר השׂכּל, discipline binds understanding to itself as its consequence, Pro 1:3. Line second repeats itself, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.12">Pro 18:12</reference>, “Pride comes before the fall.” Luther’s “And ere one comes to honour, he must previously suffer,” renders עני rather than ענוה. But the Syr. reverses the idea: the honour of the humble goeth before him, as also one of the anonymous Greek versions: προπορεύεται δὲ ταπεινοῖς δόξα. But the δόξα comes, as the above proverb expresses it, afterwards. The way to the height lies through the depth, the depth of humility under the hand of God, and, as ענוה expresses, of self-humiliation.  <chapter eID="Prov.15"/> <div eID="gen11203" type="x-p"/>
